subtopics.title: Ferrous metals and carbon content
subtopics.theory_md:
Engineering metals are **ferrous** (iron is the main constituent) or **non-ferrous**. Ferrous metals are graded by carbon:
- **Wrought iron**: below 0.1% C, soft, ductile, forgeable.
- **Mild (low carbon) steel**: 0.05 to 0.3% C; workshop jobs, bolts, structural sections.
- **Medium carbon steel**: 0.3 to 0.6% C; shafts, axles, rails.
- **High carbon steel**: 0.6 to 1.5% C; files, chisels, punches, hacksaw blades, springs.
- **Cast iron**: 2 to 4.5% C; brittle, strong in compression, damps vibration; machine beds, surface plates, vice bodies.
- **Alloy steels**: stainless steel (about 10.5% Cr or more); HSS (18% W, 4% Cr, 1% V) for drills and taps.
subtopics.basics_md: Pure iron is soft. Adding carbon makes it harder but more brittle, so the more carbon, the harder the tool and the harder it is to bend.
key_points: Ferrous = iron-based; carbon decides the grade
Mild steel 0.05-0.3% C is the fitting-shop job material
High carbon steel 0.6-1.5% C makes the cutting tools
Cast iron 2-4.5% C: brittle, good in compression, damps vibration
HSS (18-4-1 W-Cr-V) for drills and taps

subtopics.title: Non-ferrous metals and alloys
subtopics.theory_md:
**Non-ferrous** metals have no iron or only a little: aluminium (light, 2.7 g/cc), copper (wires), zinc (galvanising), lead, tin, nickel. They generally do not rust, are non-magnetic, good conductors and costlier than steel.

Common alloys:
- **Brass**: copper + zinc.
- **Bronze**: copper + tin.
- **Gunmetal**: copper + tin + zinc.
- **Solder**: tin + lead.
- **Duralumin**: aluminium + copper + magnesium + manganese.

| Ferrous | Non-ferrous |
|---|---|
| Iron main constituent | Iron absent or minor |
| Mostly magnetic, rust | Non-magnetic, corrosion resistant |
| Cheaper, stronger | Costlier, lighter, better conductors |
subtopics.basics_md: Remember brass = copper + zinc, bronze = copper + tin. Bearings and bells are bronze.
key_points: Non-ferrous: no iron, non-magnetic, corrosion resistant, costlier

subtopics.title: Mechanical property words
subtopics.theory_md:
Property words examiners ask in one or two marks:
- **Ductility**: drawn into wire under tension (copper, mild steel).
- **Malleability**: hammered or rolled into sheet under compression (gold, aluminium, lead).
- **Hardness**: resistance to scratching or indentation.
- **Toughness**: absorbs energy and deforms before fracture, resists impact (mild steel).
- **Brittleness**: breaks with little plastic deformation (cast iron, glass).
- **Elasticity**: returns to shape when the load is removed. **Plasticity**: keeps the new shape.
subtopics.basics_md: Think of copper wire (pulled, ductile) and aluminium foil (flattened, malleable).
key_points: Ductility is under tension (wire); malleability under compression (sheet)
Toughness = energy absorbed before fracture; cast iron is hard but not tough
Brittleness is the opposite of ductility
Hardness = resistance to indentation or scratching

subtopics.title: Bench vice
subtopics.theory_md:
The **bench vice** (parallel-jaw vice) holds the job for filing, sawing, chipping and tapping.

**Parts**: cast iron **body** bolted to the bench; **fixed jaw**; **movable jaw** sliding in a guide; **square-threaded screw** with **nut**, turned by a **handle**; hardened, serrated **jaw plates**.

**Size** is the **width of the jaws** (75 to 150 mm). Fix the vice so the jaw top is at elbow height. Hold the job low, near the jaws, to stop chatter. Put **soft jaws** (aluminium, copper, lead caps) over the plates to protect a finished surface. The square thread gives high axial force for little friction and wear.
subtopics.basics_md: A vice is a very strong screw clamp. Turning the handle drives the screw, which pushes the movable jaw against the fixed one with the job between.
key_points: Parts: body, fixed jaw, movable jaw, jaw plates, square-threaded screw, nut, handle
Size = width of jaws, e.g. 100 mm
Soft jaws (Al, Cu, Pb) protect finished surfaces
Job held low and close to the jaws; vice at elbow height

subtopics.title: V-block
subtopics.theory_md:
A **V-block** is a hardened steel or cast iron block with an accurately machined **90 degree V-groove**, usually on top and bottom, with side grooves and a slot for a U-clamp.

**Use**: a round bar lying in the V has its axis parallel to the base. It holds cylindrical work on the surface plate for **marking centre lines** and centres with a surface gauge or height gauge, and under the drill for **drilling across a shaft**. V-blocks are made as **matched pairs** so a long shaft lies parallel to the plate.
subtopics.basics_md: The V acts like a cradle: two sloping faces centre a round bar automatically, whatever its diameter.
key_points: Block with 90 degree V-groove, hardened and ground
Holds round work for marking and drilling
Used in matched pairs with a U-clamp

subtopics.title: Marking out and marking tools
subtopics.theory_md:
**Marking (marking out)** is drawing the layout of the job, lines, centres and curves, on the metal to show where metal is to be removed.

**Tools**: **scriber** (hardened steel, point about 15 degrees) for fine lines; **divider** and **trammel** for circles, arcs and stepping off; **centre punch** (90 degrees) and **prick punch** (30 degrees) for dots; **surface gauge** (base, pillar, scriber) for lines parallel to the plate; **odd-leg caliper**; **try square**; steel rule.

**Reference**: **surface plate** (cast iron or granite, flat top) is the datum; **V-block** and **angle plate** hold the job. **Marking media**: chalk (rough), marking blue (finished), copper sulphate (bright steel).
subtopics.basics_md: Marking is like tracing the drawing onto the metal so the file knows where to stop.
key_points: Marking = transferring the drawing to the job as lines and dots
Scriber, divider, odd-leg caliper, punches, surface gauge, try square
Surface plate is the flat datum; V-block and angle plate hold the job

subtopics.title: Measuring tools and checking tools
subtopics.theory_md:
Measuring tools give a size to a stated accuracy:
- **Steel rule**: least count 0.5 mm (or 1 mm).
- **Calipers** (inside, outside): transfer sizes; read on a rule.
- **Vernier caliper**: 0.02 mm. **Micrometer**: 0.01 mm.
- **Vernier height and depth gauge**, **dial gauge**, **feeler gauge** (gaps), **radius gauge**, **screw pitch gauge**, **bevel protractor**.
- **Try square**: checks 90 degrees (stock and blade). **Straight edge**: long, flat bar to check flatness or straightness by light gaps, or to guide a scriber.

|---|---|
| Transfer dimensions to the job | Find the size of a feature |
| Accuracy about 0.25 mm | Accuracy 0.02 or 0.01 mm |
| Scriber, divider, punches | Rule, vernier, micrometer |
| Leave a mark on the job | Leave no mark |

subtopics.title: Classification and families of fitting tools
subtopics.theory_md:
Fitting tools are classified by function:
1. **Holding**: bench vice, hand vice, pipe vice, V-block, clamps, angle plate.
2. **Marking and measuring**: scriber, divider, odd-leg caliper, punches, surface plate, surface gauge, try square, steel rule, vernier caliper, micrometer.
3. **Cutting**: files, chisels, hacksaw, drills, taps, dies, reamers, scrapers.
4. **Striking**: ball peen, cross peen, straight peen hammers, mallet.
5. **Miscellaneous**: spanners, screwdrivers, pliers, file card, oil can.

**Carpentry**: marking and measuring (rule, try square, marking and mortise gauge, bevel); cutting (rip saw, cross-cut saw, tenon saw, chisels, planes); boring (brace and bit, gimlet); striking (mallet, claw hammer); holding (carpenter's vice, bench hook, sash clamp).

**Templates and jigs**: a **template** is a profile gauge the job is checked against; a **jig** holds the work and guides the tool. They give repeatability and interchangeability.

subtopics.title: Why marking and measuring matter; shop safety
subtopics.theory_md:
**Significance**: marking tools transfer the drawing to the job as visible lines and dots; measuring tools check the size is reached. They give the **datum**, let the job be checked at each stage, reduce rework and scrap, and ensure **interchangeability**. **Precision** is repeatability; **accuracy** is closeness to the true size.

**Safety in the fitting shop**: wear safety shoes and goggles, no loose clothing; clamp the job firmly; never use a file without a handle (the tang can pierce the palm); do not use chisels or punches with mushroomed heads; do not blow filings with the mouth, use a brush; keep the floor clean; know the fire and first-aid points.
subtopics.basics_md: A cut can be corrected only if you know how far off you are, which is why you measure often.
key_points: Marking and measuring give the datum, stage checks, less scrap and interchangeability
Precision = repeatability; accuracy = closeness to true size

topics.topic: Files, chisels, hacksaw, punches and hammers

subtopics.title: Files
subtopics.theory_md:
A **file** is a hardened high carbon steel bar with rows of cutting teeth. **Parts**: tang, heel, face, edge, point; **length is measured from heel to point, without the tang**.

**By cut**: single-cut (soft metals, finish), double-cut (fast removal on steel), rasp-cut (wood, leather), curved-cut (soft metals).
**By grade** (coarse to fine): rough, bastard, second cut, smooth, dead smooth.
**By shape**: **flat** (general flat surfaces), **hand** (one safe edge), **square** (square holes, slots), **round** (rat tail; enlarging round holes), **half-round** (curves and flats), **triangular** (corners over 60 degrees, saw sharpening), **knife-edge** (narrow grooves, acute angles), needle files.

**Pinning** is clogging of teeth by metal; clear it with a file card.
subtopics.basics_md: Every tooth is a tiny chisel. Many teeth in a row remove metal in thin shavings, so a file can finish a surface smoothly.
key_points: Parts: tang, heel, face, edge, point; length without tang
Cut: single, double, rasp, curved; grade: rough, bastard, second cut, smooth, dead smooth
Shapes: flat, hand, square, round, half-round, triangular, knife-edge
Hand file has one safe edge; triangular file for corners over 60 degrees

subtopics.title: Hacksaw: blades and cutting process
subtopics.theory_md:
**Saws in the fitting shop**: hand hacksaw (fixed or adjustable frame), junior hacksaw, power hacksaw, band saw, circular saw, coping saw.

**Blade**: HSS or high carbon steel, 250 or 300 mm. **All-hard** (brittle, straight cuts); **flexible** (only the teeth hardened). **Pitch** (teeth per 25 mm): 14 coarse (soft metals, thick sections), 18 to 24 (mild steel, tubes), 32 (thin sheet, hard steel). Keep at least 2 to 3 teeth in contact. **Set** (raker or wavy) makes the kerf wider than the blade.

**Process**: teeth point **forward**, blade taut; job low and near the vice jaws; start with a nick; cut on the **forward stroke** only, 40 to 60 strokes per minute, full blade length; saw in the waste, about 1 mm from the line; ease off at the end.

**Pitch** $p = 25.4/n$ mm.
subtopics.basics_md: The saw cuts like a file does: pushing forward bites, pulling back must glide, so the teeth face away from you.
key_points: Teeth point forward; cuts on the forward stroke; 40-60 strokes per minute
Pitch: 14 tpi soft/thick, 18-24 mild steel, 32 thin sheet/tubes
At least 2-3 teeth in contact with the section
Set gives kerf clearance so the blade does not bind
All-hard blade is brittle; flexible blade has hardened teeth only

questions.q: A hacksaw blade has 18 teeth per 25.4 mm. Find its pitch and say whether it suits a 1.5 mm thick sheet.
questions.model_answer_md:
$p = \dfrac{25.4}{18} = 1.41$ mm.

Teeth in contact $= t/p = 1.5/1.41 \approx 1.06$, only about one tooth. At least 2 to 3 teeth are needed, so the blade is **not suitable**. Use 32 teeth per 25.4 mm: $p = 25.4/32 = 0.79$ mm, giving about 1.9 teeth on 1.5 mm (about 2).

subtopics.title: Chisels and punches
subtopics.theory_md:
A **chisel** is a hardened and tempered steel tool struck with a hammer to **chip** metal, cut rivet heads, bolts and sheet, and cut grooves.

**Types**:
- **Flat (cold) chisel**: flat surfaces, sheet, rivet heads.
- **Cross-cut (cape) chisel**: narrow edge; keyways and narrow grooves.
- **Half-round (round nose) chisel**: oil grooves, curved grooves.
- **Diamond-point chisel**: V-grooves, corners.
- **Side chisel**: slots at the side.

Cutting angle about **60 degrees** for mild steel (larger for harder metal). Hold at 35 to 40 degrees to the surface; watch the cutting edge; wear goggles.

**Punches**: **prick punch** 30 degrees (light layout dots); **centre punch** 90 degrees (centre mark to start a drill).

subtopics.title: Outside, inside and odd-leg calipers
subtopics.theory_md:
Calipers have **no scale**: they are set to the work and then read against a steel rule (or set from the rule and offered to the job). They are **transfer (indirect) measuring** instruments, accurate to about 0.25 mm and dependent on the user's 'feel'.
- **Outside caliper**: legs bowed inwards; outside diameters and thickness.
- **Inside caliper**: legs straight, tips turned outwards; bores and slot widths.
- **Odd-leg (hermaphrodite, jenny) caliper**: one bent leg and one pointed leg; scribes a line parallel to a finished edge and finds the centre of a round bar.

Size = length from the pivot to the tip. The legs should just touch and slide over the work under their own weight; forcing them gives a wrong reading.
subtopics.basics_md: A caliper only remembers a gap. You copy the gap from the job onto a rule to read it.
key_points: Calipers are indirect: set to the job, read on a steel rule
Outside caliper: legs curve inwards; inside caliper: tips turn outwards
Odd-leg caliper: lines parallel to an edge, centre of a round bar
Accuracy about 0.25 mm; correct feel, never force

subtopics.title: Dividers and joint construction
subtopics.theory_md:
**Dividers** have two straight legs with hardened, sharp points. Uses: **scribing circles and arcs**, **stepping off equal distances**, transferring lengths from a steel rule.

**Construction**:
- **Firm-joint**: legs held by friction at a riveted joint; set by tapping on the bench.
- **Spring-joint**: bow spring with screw and nut; finer setting and holds it.

**Size** = length from the joint to the tip, e.g. 150 mm. Do not use a divider to measure a diameter (that is the caliper's job) and do not use an odd-leg caliper for a bore.

subtopics.title: Drilling, boring and the twist drill
subtopics.theory_md:
**Drilling** makes a round hole in solid metal with a rotating **twist drill** fed along its axis. **Boring** enlarges and finishes an existing hole to a precise size, straightness and finish with a single-point tool.

**Classification of drills**: by shape (twist, flat or spade, straight-fluted, centre, core, step); by shank (straight, **Morse taper** with tang); by material (HSS, carbon steel, carbide-tipped).

**Twist drill parts**: shank, tang, neck, body with two helical **flutes** (carry chips and coolant), **lands** (margin: guides and sizes the hole), **web**, **chisel edge** (dead centre), two **lips**. **Point angle 118 degrees**, **helix angle** about 30 degrees, **lip clearance** 8 to 12 degrees.

Spindle speed: $N = \dfrac{1000\,V}{\pi D}$ rpm, $D$ in mm, $V$ in m/min.
subtopics.basics_md: A drill is a rotating wedge pair: the two lips cut, the flutes carry the chips up and out.
key_points: Drilling = round hole in solid; boring = enlarging and finishing an existing hole
Parts: shank, neck, body, flutes, lands, web, chisel edge, two lips
Point angle 118 degrees, helix about 30 degrees, lip clearance 8-12 degrees
Taper shank (Morse) has a tang; straight shank is held in a chuck

subtopics.title: Taps, tapping and tap drill size
subtopics.theory_md:
**Tapping** cuts an **internal thread** in a drilled hole using a **tap** held in a **tap wrench**. A set has three taps of one size: **taper (first)** with a long lead to start the thread, **second (intermediate)**, and **plug (bottoming)** that cuts full threads to the bottom of a blind hole.

$d = D - p$ (metric thread, major diameter $D$, pitch $p$), e.g. M10 x 1.5: $10 - 1.5 = 8.5$ mm.

**Method**: centre punch, drill, chamfer the mouth, start the tap square, **half turn forward, quarter turn back** to break the chip, cutting oil, then second and plug taps. Check with a bolt.

A **reamer** is a multi-toothed tool that enlarges a drilled hole by 0.1 to 0.5 mm and gives an **accurate size, smooth finish, round and straight hole**. **Types**: hand reamer (straight or spiral flutes, square end for a tap wrench), machine (chucking) reamer, taper reamer (for taper pins), adjustable reamer, expanding reamer, shell reamer.

topics.topic: Vernier caliper: principle, least count, reading

subtopics.title: Principle and least count
subtopics.theory_md:
A vernier caliper reads to 0.02 mm (or 0.05, 0.1 mm), far better than a rule's 0.5 mm.

**Principle**: two scales with slightly different divisions. $n$ vernier divisions (VSD) equal $(n-1)$ main scale divisions (MSD), so one VSD is shorter than one MSD.

$LC = 1\ \mathrm{MSD} - 1\ \mathrm{VSD} = \dfrac{s}{n}$ ($s$ = value of one MSD).
- 10 VSD = 9 mm: $LC = 1/10 = 0.1$ mm.
- 20 VSD = 19 mm: $LC = 1/20 = 0.05$ mm.
- 50 VSD = 49 mm: $LC = 1/50 = 0.02$ mm.

**Parts**: beam with main scale, fixed jaw, sliding jaw with vernier, upper (inside) jaws, lower (outside) jaws, depth rod, locking and fine-adjustment screws. Measures outside, inside and depth.
subtopics.basics_md: The vernier lets you read between two lines of the main scale by seeing which vernier line lines up with a main line.
key_points: n VSD = (n - 1) MSD
LC = 1 MSD - 1 VSD = s / n
50 divisions on 49 mm gives 0.02 mm; 20 on 19 gives 0.05; 10 on 9 gives 0.1
Parts: main scale, vernier, fixed and sliding jaws, upper jaws, depth rod, lock screw
Measures outside, inside and depth

questions.model_answer_md:
$1\ \mathrm{MSD} = 0.5$ mm. $1\ \mathrm{VSD} = \dfrac{24 \times 0.5}{25} = 0.48$ mm.

$LC = 0.5 - 0.48 = 0.02$ mm.
(Equivalent: $LC = s/n = 0.5/25 = 0.02$ mm.)

LC = 1 MSD - 1 VSD

subtopics.title: Taking a reading and zero error
subtopics.theory_md:
**Reading**: close the jaws and note the zero error; place the job; read the **main scale reading (MSR)** just before the vernier zero; find the vernier division that coincides with a main scale line (**VSC**).

$\text{Reading} = \mathrm{MSR} + \mathrm{VSC} \times LC \pm \text{zero error}$

**Zero error** (jaws closed): vernier zero to the **right** of main zero is **positive**, error $= +\mathrm{VSC}\times LC$, subtracted. Vernier zero to the **left** is **negative**, error $= -(n - \mathrm{VSC})\times LC$, added.

Corrected reading = observed reading - zero error (with sign).

**Micrometer** (one-line recall): reading = sleeve + thimble x 0.01 mm; LC $= 0.5/50 = 0.01$ mm.
subtopics.basics_md: The scale line just left of the vernier zero gives whole millimetres; the matching vernier line gives the leftover fraction.
key_points: Reading = MSR + VSC x LC
Positive zero error (vernier zero right of main zero): subtract
Negative zero error: -(n - VSC) x LC; add
Avoid parallax and over-tightening the jaws

Zero error $= +3 \times 0.02 = +0.06$ mm (positive, zero to the right).

Observed $= 30 + 14 \times 0.02 = 30.28$ mm.

True diameter $= 30.28 - 0.06 = 30.22$ mm.

Observed = 30.28 mm

subtopics.title: Screw principle, parts and least count
subtopics.theory_md:
The **outside micrometer (screw gauge)** reads to **0.01 mm**.

**Principle**: screw and nut. One full turn of the thimble moves the spindle by one **pitch**. If the thimble has $n$ divisions, one division moves the spindle by pitch/$n$:
$LC = \dfrac{\text{pitch}}{n} = \dfrac{0.5}{50} = 0.01$ mm.

**Parts**: U-shaped **frame**; **anvil** (fixed); **spindle** (moving); **sleeve (barrel)** with the datum line and main scale; **thimble** with the circular scale; **ratchet stop** (constant measuring pressure); **lock nut**. Range is 25 mm per micrometer (0-25, 25-50 and so on). Always close with the ratchet.
subtopics.basics_md: Turning a screw one full turn moves it forward by its pitch. A big circular scale on the thimble lets you read tiny fractions of one turn.
key_points: Principle: screw and nut; one turn = one pitch
LC = pitch / thimble divisions = 0.5/50 = 0.01 mm
Parts: frame, anvil, spindle, sleeve, thimble, ratchet, lock nut

subtopics.title: Taking a reading and zero error
subtopics.theory_md:
**Reading** $=$ sleeve reading (whole mm, plus 0.5 mm if the half-mm line is visible) $+$ thimble division on the datum line $\times 0.01$ mm.

**Zero error** (faces closed): thimble zero **below** the datum line, division $x$ on the line: error $= +x \times LC$, **subtract**. Thimble zero **not reached**, division $x$ on the line: error $= -(n - x)\times LC$, **add**.

Missing the half-mm line is the commonest slip: 7.5 + 0.28 = 7.78, not 7.28.

Check zero by lowering the jaw on the plate. It is the precise (scaled) version of the surface gauge.

subtopics.title: Vernier depth gauge
subtopics.theory_md:
Same vernier principle and **LC 0.02 mm**.

**Parts**: a **base (stock)** with a wide flat reference face that bridges the hole or slot, a narrow graduated **beam (rod)** sliding through it, the **vernier** on the base, and a clamp screw.

topics.topic: Fitting processes: marking, chipping, sawing, filing

subtopics.title: What fitting is, and its operations
subtopics.theory_md:
**Fitting** is the assembling of parts, making them fit together with the required clearance or interference, by removing small amounts of metal with **hand tools**, without machine tools.

**Operations**: marking and measuring, holding in a vice, **chipping**, **sawing**, **filing**, scraping, **drilling**, reaming, **tapping**, **threading with a die**, bending, riveting, grinding, assembling and checking the fit.

Sheet-metal operations in a press: **punching** cuts a hole in sheet with a punch and die; the removed slug is waste. **Blanking** cuts the required piece out of the sheet; the piece is the product and the rest is scrap.
subtopics.basics_md: The fitter does by hand, with file and saw, what a machine does by power. It is used where one or two parts must fit exactly.
key_points: Fitting = assembling parts by hand-tool metal removal to the required fit

Punching: hole is the product; blanking: the cut piece is the product

subtopics.title: Marking out, chipping and sawing in a job
subtopics.theory_md:
**Marking**: check stock; file two adjacent edges flat and square as **datum edges**; coat with marking blue; mark all lines from the datum with scriber, rule, try square or height gauge; put **witness marks** with a prick punch along the lines (half the dot should remain after filing); centre-punch hole centres.

**Chipping**: remove metal with a cold chisel and ball peen hammer; chisel at 35 to 40 degrees; watch the cutting edge, wear goggles, use a chipping screen.

**Sawing**: job low in the vice, line near the jaws; start with a nick; forward stroke cuts, 40 to 50 strokes per minute; **saw in the waste**, about 1 mm from the line, then file to the line.
subtopics.basics_md: You always leave a little extra metal at each stage and remove it in the next, finer stage.
key_points: Datum edges first, then marking from them

3. Mark lines from the datum with scriber, steel rule, try square, surface gauge or height gauge.
4. Put witness marks along the lines with a prick punch.
5. Centre-punch the hole centres.
6. Check the marked dimensions.

subtopics.title: Filing operations, files, templates and jigs
subtopics.theory_md:
**Filing** removes a small amount of metal with a file. The job is held in the vice at elbow level; the file is held with both hands and pushed forward with light downward pressure on the **cutting stroke**, lifted on the return (40 to 50 strokes per minute). Keep the file level; rocking makes the surface convex. Check with the try square against light; clean the file with a file card.

**Operations**: **cross (straight) filing** for rough removal and flattening; **draw filing** (file held at right angles to the job and moved sideways along it) for a fine finish; **lathe filing** on a rotating job; also level, square, flat and curved filing.

**Template**: profile gauge to check shape. **Jig**: holds the work and guides the tool. They ensure **consistency** (repeatability, interchangeability, speed).
subtopics.basics_md: Cross filing takes the metal off; draw filing polishes what is left.
key_points: Pressure on the forward stroke only; lift on the return
Cross filing for removal; draw filing for finish

subtopics.title: Sequence of a complete fitting job
subtopics.theory_md:
**Typical sequence** (MS flat, L-shape or square fit):
1. Study the drawing; select and inspect the stock.
2. File one face and edge flat and square (datum).
3. Apply marking blue; mark lines with scriber, rule, try square, surface gauge; punch.
4. Hold in vice; **saw** about 1 mm outside the line.
5. **Chip** if needed with chisel and hammer.
6. **File** rough then smooth to the lines; check size with vernier or micrometer and flatness with the try square.
7. **Drill, tap or ream** where required.
8. **Trial fit** with the mating piece, trim using marking blue and light.
9. Deburr, finish, clean, oil.

For an **L-shape sheet** joint: cut the sheet to size with shears or hacksaw, file edges, mark the bend line and holes, **bend to 90 degrees in a vice** with a mallet, drill and rivet or bolt.
subtopics.basics_md: Plan the job as a flow chart: each box is one operation whose output feeds the next.
key_points: Study drawing, prepare datum, mark, saw, chip, file, drill/tap, trial fit, finish
